summary.one_line: A three-season-old, single-plant jaggery-powder processor in Dharashiv (Maharashtra) selling commodity product to a handful of B2B buyers. Most of the Rs.93.66 crore fresh issue repays bank debt. Profit growth is real on paper, but cash conversion is weak, there is no moat, and the governance record is poor: a long list of compliance lapses, sizeable promoter loans and dealings with promoter-linked entities. The case to apply is not strong enough.
bull_points: Fast reported growth: revenue from operations rose from Rs.36.28 crore (FY24, a part-season year) to Rs.58.57 crore (FY25) and Rs.75.27 crore (FY26). Restated PAT rose from Rs.3.08 crore to Rs.5.50 crore to Rs.11.59 crore (S1, S8).

The plant runs close to full during the crushing season: crushing utilisation was 92.78%, 83.84% and 93.53% in FY24-FY26, and jaggery-powder utilisation was 94.09% in FY26. That gives a real operational reason to expand from 1,250 to 2,000 TCD (S1).
Entirely a fresh issue (no OFS), so all money goes to the company. Rs.48.50 crore repays secured bank and FI debt and none of it repays promoter loans (S3, S11).

Sugarcane comes from a fragmented farmer base (top 10 suppliers were only 3.03% of purchases), and the company sells by-products (bagasse, molasses, press mud, ash) and generates captive power from bagasse (S11, S8).

The Maharashtra PSI-2019 incentive certificate for the Khamaswadi facility covers 1 January 2024 to 30 April 2035, with admissible incentives of Rs.43.50 crore. Rs.2.82 crore was accrued in FY26 (S11, S1).
bear_points: Extreme customer concentration: the top 5 customers were 97.45% of revenue in the April-July 2026 stub period and 63.67% in FY26. Madhya Pradesh alone was 79.11% of stub revenue (S1).

One-product business: jaggery powder was 86.28% of FY26 product sales and 94.46% in the stub period. The 'Feel Guddy' B2C premix line shrank from Rs.4.40 crore (FY25) to Rs.0.95 crore (FY26) to Rs.0.04 crore (stub) (S1).
Profit is not turning into cash: cumulative operating cash flow over FY24-FY26 was about Rs.0.5 crore (-17.79 + 13.24 + 5.04) against cumulative PAT of about Rs.20.2 crore (S1, S8).

Long compliance-lapse record: 27 delayed ROC filings (one 1,098 days late), repeated GST/PF/TDS/professional-tax delays, ESIC deductions started only in March 2026 despite registration in June 2022, and a pending adjudication for a 2024 private placement done without the required valuation report (S1).

Promoter-linked dealings: Rs.25.45 crore of unsecured loans from the two promoter-directors, repayable on demand. Loans of Rs.9.19 crore (FY24), Rs.8.65 crore (FY25) and Rs.9.21 crore (FY26) were taken from and repaid to the promoters' earlier similar-business company in the same year. Harvesting and transport bills are paid to the MD, the general manager and a relative, and the factory is leased from the CFO-promoter (S1).
watch_points: Whether the FY26 margin holds. EBITDA margin was 27.19% in FY26 but 13.35% in the off-season stub, and the company itself says the PAT-margin jump 'may not be sustainable' (S3, S1).
Capex execution: no equipment order has been placed. The Rs.19.95 crore + GST quotation is dated 11 November 2026 and completion is targeted for December 2027 (S1, S11).
Outcome of the Section 62(1)(c) adjudication (GNL-1 filed 12 June 2026) and any further statutory-filing delays once listed (S1).
Sugarcane price and season length: the factory ran 146, 102 and 120 days in FY24-FY26 at average cane prices of about Rs.2,800, Rs.2,500 and Rs.2,650 per MT (S1).

reasoning: The money mostly fixes the balance sheet rather than building the business. Rs.48.50 crore of the stated Rs.72.04 crore of objects repays secured bank/FI debt, against Rs.23.54 crore for a capex project with no order placed yet. Deleveraging is sensible for a company whose debt-to-equity was 5.89x in FY24, but new shareholders are largely paying to clean up past leverage (S3, S11, S1).

There is no moat. The product is commodity jaggery powder sold B2B, mostly to a few traders/processors: top 5 customers were 97.45% of stub revenue and two states took almost all of it. The branded B2C line has nearly vanished (Rs.0.04 crore in the stub). The RHP's own industry chapter shows khandsari output collapsing nationally. Listed comparables are other small sugar/jaggery processors, with no technical or regulatory barrier (S1, S6).

Earnings quality is unproven. Only two full crushing seasons are on record. FY26 PAT includes Rs.2.82 crore of state incentive accruals and other income of Rs.3.05 crore. Three-year cumulative operating cash flow was near zero against roughly Rs.20 crore of reported PAT. The off-season stub margin was half the FY26 level (S1, S11).

Governance is the deciding negative. The RHP discloses dozens of delayed statutory filings, a pending private-placement contravention, and a promoter whose DIN was disqualified from 2016 to 2021 after his earlier company was struck off. He is also the sitting BJP Dharashiv district president. Recurring same-year loans in and out of a similar-business company the promoters only exited in July 2026, plus payments to the MD for harvesting and transport, call for a level of trust this record has not earned (S1).

The structure leaves outside investors exposed. Promoters keep 65% post-issue, and only 20.16% is locked for three years: 42.25 lakh shares unlock after one year and another 42.25 lakh after two. Promoter acquisition cost is Rs.4.00 and Rs.0.19 per share, mostly via a June 2026 bonus. The minimum retail ticket is Rs.2.84 lakh in an illiquid SME stock (S1, S3).

subsections.title: What the company makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Shree Siddhivinayak Greentech was incorporated on 24 June 2022 and converted to a public company in March 2026 (S12). It crushes sugarcane and turns the juice into jaggery powder, plus khandsari sugar since FY26. It also sells jaggery-based instant premixes (tea, coffee, rice kheer, laddoo, lapsi) under the 'Feel Guddy' brand, sugarcane seed from its own nursery, and by-products: bagasse, molasses, press mud and ash (S4, S1). Factory operations for jaggery powder began in FY24, premixes in FY25, and khandsari and cane seeds in FY26 (S12, S1).

In practice this is a B2B jaggery-powder business. B2B sales were 99.90% of revenue from operations in the April-July 2026 stub period, and B2C sales were only Rs.3.64 lakh (S11). Buyers are wholesalers, distributors and industrial users (S8). The khandsari brand 'Simply Sakhar' is still only a plan (S8). Revenue is booked as product sales at prevailing market prices. The RHP describes the products as commodities with no long-term offtake contracts, so realisations move with the jaggery/sugar cycle (S9, S11).

blocks.caption: Product sales mix, Rs. crore (share of product sales) - restated, from RHP risk factor 1 (S1)

blocks.text: The product-diversification story in the marketing material is not in the numbers. The branded premix line fell about 78% in FY26 and was almost nil in the stub. Khandsari was about 1% of FY26 sales on 8% capacity utilisation. Cane seeds are a one-year Rs.5.66 crore item. The business is jaggery powder (S1).

There is one leased manufacturing facility in Maharashtra. The incentive certificate refers to it as the Khamaswadi facility, and the registered office is in Osmanabad/Dharashiv (S11, S8). The factory, registered office and warehouses are all leased (S8). One factory lease, from promoter Dattatray Kulkarni, runs to July 2042 at Rs.50,000 a month with a 10% step-up every three years (S11). The crushing season runs roughly October/November to April/May. The factory ran 146 days in FY24, 102 in FY25 and 120 in FY26, and crushing for FY27 had not started by 31 July 2026 (S1).

'Installed capacity' here is daily rated capacity (1,250 TCD) times operating days, so a short cane season shrinks reported capacity rather than lowering utilisation. Real output still swings with the season: cane crushed fell 36.87% in FY25, when the season shortened to 102 days, then rose 31.25% in FY26 (S1). The company employed 155 permanent staff at 31 March 2026 and uses contract labour in season (S3, S9).

subsections.title: Customers, suppliers and the supply chain

blocks.text: Sugarcane is bought directly from farmers near the plant under seasonal arrangements, with no long-term contracts and no hedging. The supplier base is highly fragmented: the top 10 suppliers were just 3.03% of purchases (S1, S11). Separate seasonal contractors harvest and transport the cane. That cost was Rs.14.48 crore in FY26 (19.23% of revenue) on top of cane purchases of Rs.36.89 crore (49.01%), so together the two were 68.24% of FY26 revenue (S1, S11). Some harvesting and transport bills were paid to related parties: Rs.49.88 lakh to MD Dipali Kulkarni, Rs.16.04 lakh to the general manager and Rs.9.66 lakh to promoter-group member Mangesh Kulkarni in FY26 (S1).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration - share of revenue from operations (S1)
Revenue by state, share of revenue from operations (S1)

blocks.text: The off-season pattern shows how the model works. Cane is crushed and inventory built between November and March, then liquidated over the following months. In the stub period inventories fell by Rs.28.26 crore and almost all of it went to five buyers, mostly in Madhya Pradesh (S1). Customers are not named in the sources reviewed. The RHP says the loss of one or more of them could materially hurt revenue (S1).

The RHP's industry chapter was commissioned by the lead manager from Infomerics Analytics & Research for a fee (S9). It frames demand around substitution of refined sugar, convenience premixes and clean-label trends, but gives qualitative 'High/Moderate' driver ratings rather than a jaggery market size (S1). Raw-material supply is ample: Indian sugarcane output is estimated at about 5,002 lakh tonnes in FY26 (2nd advance estimate), up from 4,546 lakh tonnes in FY25 (S1).

Third-party estimates vary widely with scope. IMARC values the Indian packaged-jaggery market at INR 79.63 billion in 2025 and projects an 11.22% CAGR over 2026-2034, with North India the largest region at 30% (S16). Other vendors publish figures that differ by orders of magnitude, which suggests units or scope problems (S20). Most of this company's output is bulk B2B powder, not packaged consumer jaggery, so the packaged-market growth rate is at best a loose proxy.

Khandsari, the company's newest line, is a shrinking national category. The RHP cites USDA data showing khandsari production falling from about 5.3 lakh MT in 2020-21 to 75,000 MT in 2023-24 and about 60,000 MT in 2024-25 (S1). Instant premix/ready-to-eat production grew from about 4.94 lakh tonnes to about 7.33 lakh tonnes between FY20 and FY25 (S1). That is the segment where the company's own sales have collapsed.

The listed peers named in the offer documents are Dhampure Specialty Sugars and Dollex Agrotech, both small listed sugar/jaggery processors (S6, S18). In packaged jaggery, IMARC lists Dhampur Green, Patanjali, Two Brothers Organic Farms, Organic Tattva, 24 Mantra Organic and others (S16). Bulk jaggery powder is also made by many unorganised local crushers in cane belts. One of the company's own independent directors is an independent director of M.V.K. Agro Food Product Ltd, which manufactures sugar (S1).

items: No market-share claim, import-substitution claim or 'only Indian maker' claim appears in the sources reviewed. The aggregator summary says competitors are not named and no market-share data is given (S9).

The cited strengths are generic: proximity to cane, backward integration through a cane-seed nursery, a zero-waste by-product model, and captive bagasse power (S10, S8). Any well-sited cane processor shares these features.

The one firm-specific economic advantage is the Maharashtra PSI-2019 incentive (Rs.43.50 crore admissible until April 2035). That is a subsidy rather than a competitive barrier, and it is tied to this facility (S11).
Pricing power looks absent. The company has no hedging and no long-term contracts, and it depends on a few traders and processors who can switch suppliers (S1, S11).

blocks.text: Plain assessment: there is no genuine moat. This is a well-utilised, regional commodity processor whose returns depend on cane prices, season length and a handful of buyers.

blocks.caption: Restated P&L, Rs. crore (S1; also S3, S8)

blocks.text: Revenue grew 61.44% in FY25, mostly because FY24 had only 4-5 months of sales, and 28.52% in FY26 (S1). FY26 benefited from 31% more cane crushed, the first khandsari and cane-seed sales, and a 14.42% fall in finance cost (S1). PAT more than doubled from Rs.5.50 crore to Rs.11.59 crore. The company itself warns that the FY26 PAT-margin expansion 'may not be sustainable' (S1). *The stub margin comes from aggregator KPI tables (S3).

Some of the profit is not operating profit. Other income, mostly the Maharashtra PSI-2019 subsidy accrual of Rs.2.82 crore plus interest, was Rs.3.05 crore in FY26, about 19% of PBT (S1, S11). Average cane cost was about Rs.2,650/MT in FY26 versus about Rs.2,500/MT in FY25 and Rs.2,800/MT in FY24, so a bad cane year can compress margins quickly (S1).
With only two full crushing seasons (FY25, FY26) and one partial one, a 'three-year trend' here is really a start-up ramp. It is not evidence of a durable earnings level.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, leverage and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow, Rs. crore (S1, S3, S8)

blocks.text: Leverage is high and partly informal. At 31 July 2026 secured borrowings were Rs.49.27 crore (65.94% of debt). Borrowings repayable on demand were Rs.28.99 crore, including Rs.25.45 crore of unsecured loans from the two promoter-directors and Rs.3.54 crore of cash credit (S1). HDFC Bank facilities cost 8.50-9.50%, and prepayment penalties run up to 4% (S11). The company has no active credit rating (S9). Insurance covers only about 74% of tangible assets, and there is no product-liability cover (S11).

Cash flow is the clearest red flag. Over FY24-FY26 cumulative operating cash flow was roughly Rs.0.5 crore against roughly Rs.20.2 crore of cumulative PAT (S1). In FY26 receivables rose by Rs.7.09 crore, inventory by Rs.7.84 crore and other current assets by Rs.4.25 crore, leaving operating cash flow of Rs.5.04 crore on PAT of Rs.11.59 crore (S1). The large stub-period inflow came from liquidating Rs.28.26 crore of season inventory (S1). Cash and bank balances were only about Rs.0.51 crore at 31 July 2026 (S11).

Cash-profit mismatch: reported profits have so far been absorbed by working capital and funded by debt and promoter loans. Watch FY27 receivables and operating cash flow before trusting the earnings trend.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Partly. Volumes and profit have grown, and high utilisation supports more crushing capacity (S1). Three things weaken the story. First, the off-season stub shows EBITDA margin at 13.35% against 27.19% for FY26, so the annual figure depends on the season's economics (S3). Second, the 'value-added' premix segment that would justify premium margins has shrunk to almost nothing (S1). Third, customer concentration rose sharply in the most recent period (S1).

items: Return on net worth per the RHP was 23.74%, 29.75% and 46.24% in FY24-FY26 (S1). It is flattered by a small equity base relative to Rs.75-90 crore of debt.
No dividends have been paid, and there is no formal dividend policy (S1).

Equity was built by a Rs.4.80 crore private placement in March 2024, a Rs.5 crore preference issue to 50 individuals in October 2023 (redeemed in December 2025 without dividend), and a 3:2 bonus in June 2026 out of reserves (S1).

blocks.text: The book-built SME issue is open 25-27 November 2026 at Rs.130-142 per share (face value Rs.10). It is entirely a fresh issue of 65,96,000 shares, up to Rs.93.66 crore at the upper band, with no offer for sale. Listing on NSE Emerge is tentatively 2 December 2026 (S3, S6). Erudore Capital is the book-running lead manager, MAS Services is the registrar and Basan Equity Broking is the market maker (S3).

Lot size is 1,000 shares and individuals must bid for 2 lots (2,000 shares, Rs.2,84,000 at the upper band) (S3, S8). One broker page shows the lot as 2,000 shares, which reflects the same minimum, and it also shows an inconsistent Rs.85.75 crore issue size (S10). The RHP figures above prevail. The net offer to the public is 62,66,000 shares, and post-issue share capital will be 1,88,46,000 shares, up from 1,22,50,000 (S3, S17).

blocks.caption: Use of proceeds, Rs. crore (S3, S6, S11)
rows: Capex: expand crushing from 1,250 to 2,000 TCD
Quotation Rs.19.95 cr + Rs.3.59 cr GST from N.R. Fabricators & Erectors, dated 11 Nov 2026; no order placed; completion targeted Dec 2027
About 95.96% of Rs.50.54 cr secured bank/FI debt at 31 Oct 2026; no promoter loans repaid

blocks.text: About 52% of the gross issue goes to repaying bank debt and about 25% to capex. The remaining roughly Rs.21.6 crore covers general corporate purposes and issue expenses, and the sources reviewed do not quantify the split (S3, S11). The objects have not been appraised by any bank or agency. Any capex shortfall is to come from internal accruals (S11, S9).

Being a 100% fresh issue is a plus: nothing goes to selling shareholders. The money mainly deleverages the balance sheet, though. Expected finance-cost savings (about Rs.4.1-4.6 crore a year at 8.5-9.5% on Rs.48.5 crore, analyst estimate) will lift EPS-level profit mechanically without growing the business. The growth capex is modest and not yet contracted.

The promoters are a married couple. Dipali Dattatraya Kulkarni (38, Higher Secondary Certificate) is Managing Director and holds 78.57% pre-issue. Dattatray Kashinath Kulkarni (48, B.Com) is Executive Director cum CFO and holds 21.43%. Each claims about five years of jaggery/sugar experience, and both were formally designated MD and CFO only on 19 May 2026 (S1, S19). Dattatray Kulkarni has been President of the Bharatiya Janata Party for Dharashiv district since 2 June 2025, and the RHP lists this as a risk factor (S1).

Their prior ventures overlap with this business. Both were associated with Shree Siddhivinayak Agritech Industries Ltd, which makes sugar, jaggery and by-products: Dipali as a director and Dattatray as CEO for about four years. Dipali resigned and sold her stake there only on 8 July 2026, before the IPO, 'to end conflict of interest' (S1). The promoter group also includes two co-operative credit societies that function as co-operative banks, a co-operative hospital, a housing co-op, a social foundation, and a farmer producer company with which the issuer traded (S1). Dattatray Kulkarni was a director of Kalyansagar Agro & Milk Products Pvt Ltd, which the ROC Pune struck off in 2017. His DIN was disqualified from 1 November 2016 to 31 October 2021 (S1).

items: The board has three independent directors: Brijesh Didvaniya, Mahesh Nannor and Sachin Ramgirwar. Committees were constituted on 1 June 2026 (S1).
The Company Secretary joined on 4 May 2026. The general manager, Ganesh Kamte (salary Rs.7.39 lakh in FY26), previously worked at the promoter-group credit society and at Agritech (S1).
No director remuneration was paid in FY26. Dattatray Kulkarni is now to receive Rs.1.5 lakh per month (S1).
The RHP declares the promoters are not wilful defaulters and not debarred by SEBI, and that no promoter shares are pledged (S1).

blocks.caption: Selected related-party transactions, Rs. lakh (RHP Note 28, S1)

Loan taken from / repaid to Shree Siddhivinayak Agritech (similar business)
Sales to Shree Siddhivinayak Foodtech FPC (promoter group)
Purchases from Shri Siddhivinayak Petroleum (CFO's proprietorship)
Harvest & transport bills to Dipali Kulkarni
Promoter loans outstanding at period end

blocks.text: Most of this is not routine. Promoter loans of about Rs.25.45 crore (34% of total debt) are repayable on demand, and the IPO does not repay them. That is good for the use of proceeds but leaves a large claim the promoters can call at will (S1, S11). Every year from FY24 to FY26, the company borrowed roughly Rs.9 crore from the promoters' former similar-business company and repaid the identical amount within the same year. The sources do not explain the purpose. In FY24 the company also bought Rs.3.40 crore of goods from that company and sold Rs.3.36 crore to a promoter-group producer company (S1). Paying the MD personally for harvesting and transport, and leasing the factory from the CFO, blur the line between promoter and company economics (S1).

The RPT section is not routine. It shows recurring same-year loans in and out of a sister company, trade with promoter-group entities, operating services billed by the MD, and the core plant leased from a promoter. The values are moderate relative to revenue. What matters is the pattern and how much the business depends on the promoter family.

items: Private placement non-compliance: the March 2024 allotment of 4.8 lakh shares was made without the valuation report required under Section 62(1)(c) and with incomplete explanatory-statement disclosures. The company filed GNL-1 seeking adjudication on 12 June 2026, and the hearing is pending (S1).

27 delayed ROC filings are listed. Examples: DPT-3 for FY23 filed 1,098 days late, DPT-3 for FY24 731 days late, CRA-2 404 days late and PAS-6 389 days late. Two filing errors are also disclosed (S1).

Statutory dues: GST returns delayed by up to 42 days, professional-tax returns by up to 296 days, TDS by up to 76 days, and PF and MLWF also delayed. The auditors' CARO reports for FY24 and FY25 flagged delays (S1).
ESIC: registered since 25 June 2022, but ESIC contributions were deducted and paid only from March 2026 (S1).

Litigation is small: 6 tax matters against the company (Rs.28.75 lakh), 7 against promoters (Rs.10.86 lakh), and 8 criminal cases filed by group companies (Rs.59.14 lakh). There are no material civil or criminal cases against the company (S1).
10 trademark applications have faced objections (S11).

blocks.text: Lock-in follows the post-2025 SME ICDR framework as stated in the RHP. 38,00,000 promoter shares (20.16% of post-issue capital) are locked for three years as minimum promoter contribution. Of the remaining promoter holding, 42,24,938 shares are locked for two years and 42,24,937 for one year from allotment. The 125 pre-issue shares held by non-promoters are locked for one year (S1). So about 22% of the company's post-issue equity held by promoters could become saleable after one year. The promoters' average acquisition cost is Rs.4.00 (Dipali) and Rs.0.19 (Dattatray) per share, largely because of the June 2026 bonus and a January 2026 gift of 9,99,950 shares from a relative (S1).

The company says it has fixed these lapses by hiring a whole-time Company Secretary and adopting a compliance calendar (S1). Even so, delays continued into November 2026 filings. Charge filings due 31 October 2026 and 14 November 2026 were made late (S1).

items: Customer and geographic concentration: top 5 customers were 97.45% of stub revenue and Madhya Pradesh was 79.11%. Losing one or two buyers would directly cut sales (S1).
Single commodity product: jaggery powder is 86-94% of sales, with no long-term offtake contracts and no hedging (S1, S11).

Agricultural and seasonal dependence: the crushing season varied between 102 and 146 days over three years, and cane prices swung between about Rs.2,500 and Rs.2,800/MT. Harvesting and transport rely on third-party contractors (S1).
Leverage and on-demand debt: even after the IPO, about Rs.25.45 crore of promoter loans stay repayable on demand. Weak operating cash flow means growth will likely need fresh borrowing again (S1).
Execution risk on capex: no orders have been placed, the quotation dates from November 2026, and the target is December 2027. Any slippage misses another crushing season (S1, S11).

blocks.text: These risks reinforce each other. A short cane season lowers volumes, the fixed off-season costs stay, a few buyers set price, and working capital has to be funded with debt. FY25 showed this: crush volumes fell 37% and finance cost rose 74% (S1).

items: Compliance culture: dozens of delayed statutory filings and a pending company-law contravention show the company has not reliably met basic obligations. Listed-company disclosure requirements are stricter (S1).
Related-party dependence: the plant is leased from a promoter, loans run in and out of a former similar-business sister company, and service bills are paid to the MD (S1).
Promoter profile: the CFO-promoter holds an active political post and has a past DIN disqualification. The RHP itself flags reputational risk (S1).
Margin sustainability: the company warns that the FY26 PAT margin of 15.40% may not be sustainable. The Rs.2.82 crore subsidy accrual alone was about 18% of FY26 PBT of Rs.15.87 crore (S1, S11).
SME liquidity and staggered unlocks: the minimum ticket is Rs.2.84 lakh, trading is market-maker driven, and half of the promoters' excess holding unlocks after one year (S1, S13).

blocks.text: Most of the RHP's other 60-plus risk factors (leased premises, trademark objections, labour, insurance) are standard SME boilerplate. The seven above are the ones that should drive the decision.

The concrete forward plan in the RHP is narrow. Raise crushing capacity from 1,250 TCD to 2,000 TCD (+60%), because the plant has been running at an average of about 90% of crushing capacity. Management expects jaggery-powder, khandsari and by-product output to rise 'proportionately, subject to the availability of adequate sugarcane and prevailing market conditions' (S1). The second plan is to use the IPO to repay secured borrowings, reduce finance costs and improve the debt-to-equity ratio (S1).

Beyond this, the material reviewed gives no revenue or margin guidance, no capacity targets for premixes, and no customer-diversification target. Marketing language mentions an 'emerging B2C brand presence and retail expansion' and a planned 'Simply Sakhar' khandsari brand, but no figures are attached (S10, S8). No management interview or investor call was found in the sources reviewed. A November 2026 RHP analysis likewise noted that quantified cane-seed reporting and product-wise volumes are still missing (S12).

Expanded capacity can only first affect a full season in FY29 (season starting around Oct/Nov 2027, with completion targeted December 2027). FY27 and FY28 earnings will rest on the existing 1,250 TCD plant plus interest savings.

If the debt repayment goes through, finance cost should fall meaningfully from Rs.6.86 crore (FY26), and that will support reported PAT even without volume growth (S1). Volume growth depends on cane availability in the Dharashiv catchment and on finding buyers for 60% more output. Today's customer list is tiny and the premix business has not taken off (S1). One independent IPO reviewer rates the issue only 'selective consideration for high-risk investors' (3/5), with the balance sheet scored 2/5 (S13).

items: Positive swing factors: a good cane season, stable jaggery prices, timely commissioning of the 2,000 TCD upgrade, and continued PSI-2019 incentive accruals (S1, S11).
Negative swing factors: a short or poor-recovery season, loss of a major Madhya Pradesh buyer, capex delay, or promoter loans being called (S1).

subsections.title: Day-1 subscription, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: The issue opened today (25 November 2026), so only partial day-1 data exists, and different trackers captured it at different times. At about 10:09 IST Chittorgarh showed 0.01x overall and 0.02x retail (S15). Kotak Neo showed 0.03x at 10:45 (S8). By 11:40 IST IPOJi showed 0.29x overall, with QIB 4.27x on a tiny 66,000-share QIB quota, NII 0.41x (bNII 0.60x, sNII 0.02x) and individual investors 0.09x (S7). A separate IPOWatch snapshot showed 0.15x overall (Rs.13.55 crore of bids), with NII 0.13x and retail 0.08x (S14).

No anchor book was announced. The QIB portion is just 1.05% of the net issue, and none of the sources report anchor investors (S3, S6, S8). Unofficially, grey-market trackers quoted a premium of Rs.20 on 25 November, up from Rs.0 around 19-22 November and Rs.5-10 on 23-24 November (S14, S6). Another reviewer listed Rs.10 (S13). These figures are unofficial, thinly based and volatile, and they are not used in this report's verdict.

Early QIB 'oversubscription' covers only 66,000 shares (about Rs.0.94 crore) and says little about real demand. The retail and NII books, which make up about 99% of the issue, were well below 1x when last checked. Final figures will only be known after close on 27 November 2026.

method: Primary source: the Red Herring Prospectus (S1), downloaded from the BRLM Erudore Capital's website and read directly as page images. Chapters read: capital structure, lock-in and promoter cost of acquisition (pp. 96-110), risk factors 1-18 (pp. 23-39), industry overview extracts (pp. 147-154), management and KMP (pp. 216-227), promoter and promoter group, group companies and dividend policy (pp. 228-237), related-party Note 28, capitalisation and accounting ratios (pp. 260-263), and the MD&A P&L and cash-flow discussion (pp. 281-288). The RHP's date is taken as 18 November 2026, the date of the statutory auditor's certificates it cites; the cover date was not re-verified. The objects-of-issue chapter (pp. 114-120) was opened but its detail is not retained in my notes. For that, capex/debt amounts, deployment schedule, quotation details and the share of secured debt repaid are cross-checked across Chittorgarh (S3), InvestorGain (S6), Chanakya (S13) and Multibagg's RHP summary (S11), which agree on Rs.23.54 cr capex and Rs.48.50 cr debt repayment. General corporate purposes and issue expenses could not be quantified from any source reviewed. The NSE-hosted RHP zip timed out. The DRHP on NSE archives (S2) was seen only in search results and is cited only for the filing's existence. Some figures (stub EBITDA/PAT margin, insurance cover, supplier concentration, PSI-2019 admissible amount, HDFC rates, cash balance) come from secondary RHP summaries (S3, S11) and were not re-read in the RHP itself. Industry sizing uses IMARC (S16) and is flagged as scope-inconsistent with other vendors (S20, seen in search results). Day-1 subscription is partial and comes from timestamped tracker snapshots that differ. GMP is reported only as unofficial context. Per instructions, valuation (P/E, P/B, market-cap multiples, peer multiples) is deliberately excluded even where sources volunteered it. The interest-saving estimate in the issue section is the analyst's own arithmetic from S11's quoted rates, not a company figure.
